title: KNIGHTMARE
summary: Keep the enemy king caged, use its pawns as waiting moves, and change the mating pattern when it underpromotes.

nodes.question: Why keep the enemy pawns alive?
nodes.explanation: After the rook sacrifice, two knights can cage Black’s king. The black pawns provide moves that prevent stalemate while White’s king approaches.

nodes.question: How does the promoted piece change the finish?
nodes.explanation: Black can promote a2 to a queen or a knight. White must respond to the actual attacks of that piece.

branches.title: Bring the king before the pawn promotes
commentary: Begin after ...Kxa1. The earlier eight-piece rook sacrifice is context; this seven-piece position is the checked starting point.
Nd3 controls b2. Together with Nd2 controlling b1, it leaves Black’s king no legal move.
b5 uses the available double pawn step. The blocked a-pawns cannot move while the king remains on a1.
Kg4 starts the king’s approach without disturbing the knight cage.
b4 spends another pawn step. Black’s king still has no escape.
Kf3 continues toward the corner, leaving both knights at their blocking posts.
b3 approaches the second rank, giving White one more useful move.
Ke2 brings the king within reach of d1, where it will control c1 and c2.
b2 is the last b-pawn step before promotion. White must now reshape the cage.
Nb3+ checks a1 and releases b1 while the other knight still covers b2.
Kb1 is forced. The king’s departure from a1 frees the a2 pawn to promote.
Kd1 controls c1 and c2. White completes the cage while deliberately allowing promotion.
a1=Q creates a queen, but Black’s king remains boxed in by its own pieces.
Nb4 controls a2 and c2. The queen cannot move along the first rank through its own king or along the diagonal through its own b2 pawn.
Qa2 is one of only two legal moves. It occupies the king’s a2 escape square.
Nd2+ checks b1. The queen now obstructs the square that could otherwise let the king escape.
Ka1 is forced into the corner vacated by the queen.
Nc2# checks a1. Nd2 covers b1 and b3; White’s king covers c2, and Black’s own queen and pawn occupy a2 and b2.
branches.explanation: Nc2# checks a1. Nd2 covers b1 and b3; White’s king covers c2, and Black’s own queen and pawn occupy a2 and b2.

branches.title: The queen stays home and the pawn moves
commentary: Compare Black’s other legal move after the queen promotion and knight repositioning.
a1=Q promotes, but the new queen has very little space.
Nb4 cages the king and restricts the queen, leaving only ...Qa2 or ...a2.
a2 blocks the queen’s only exit and occupies the king’s last escape square.
Nd2# checks b1. Nb4 covers a2 and c2, Kd1 covers c1, and Black’s own pieces occupy a1 and b2.
branches.explanation: Nd2# checks b1. Nb4 covers a2 and c2, Kd1 covers c1, and Black’s own pieces occupy a1 and b2.

branches.title: Meet a knight promotion with a different mate
commentary: A knight on a1 attacks different squares from a queen. White must change the move order.
a1=N attacks b3, so the quiet Nb4 plan would leave White’s other knight exposed.
Nd2+ immediately moves the attacked b3 knight with check and keeps the d3 knight ready for the final jump.
Ka2 is forced. Unlike a queen on a1, the promoted knight gives no check along the first rank.
Nb4# checks a2. Nd2 covers b1 and b3, while Black’s own knight and pawns occupy a1, a3 and b2.
branches.explanation: Nb4# checks a2. Nd2 covers b1 and b3, while Black’s own knight and pawns occupy a1, a3 and b2.

branches.title: Repeat the queen plan against a knight
commentary: Use the same quiet move against a knight and observe the different tactical result.
a1=N attacks the white knight on b3.
Nb4 ignores that attack and loses the forced win. The piece on a1 is a knight, not a boxed-in queen.
Nxb3 captures the exposed knight. The tablebase records the exact result after this source-illustrated mistake.
branches.explanation: Nxb3 captures the exposed knight. The tablebase records the exact result after this source-illustrated mistake.

exercises.prompt: Why do Black’s remaining pawns help White?
exercises.answer: They give Black legal moves while its king is caged, allowing White’s king to approach without stalemate. This does not mean two knights can force mate against a bare king.

exercises.prompt: Why must White react differently to ...a1=N?
exercises.answer: The knight attacks b3. Nd2+ moves that attacked knight with tempo; repeating Nb4 allows ...Nxb3.

startContext: Begin after ...Kxa1 at 40 seconds. The earlier eight-piece rook sacrifice is source context. The king approach, two queen-promotion mates and the knight-promotion reply are checked; other pawn tempos and promotion choices are not exhaustively displayed.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
